title: Energy, enzymes, and metabolism
note: Reactions that release free energy (exergonic, ΔG < 0) can drive reactions that need it (endergonic, ΔG > 0), usually through ATP. Enzymes speed reactions by lowering activation energy; they do not change ΔG and are not used up. Inhibitors and allosteric regulators switch enzymes on and off.

read.title: How enzymes get reactions moving
text: Many reactions in a cell release energy, yet they barely happen on their own. Sugar sitting in a bowl does not burst into carbon dioxide and water, even though that reaction is strongly exergonic. The reason is activation energy, the push needed to strain and break existing bonds before new ones can form.

Enzymes lower that barrier. Most are proteins with a pocket called the active site. When a substrate binds, the site shifts slightly to grip it, an idea called induced fit. The enzyme may bend the substrate, bring two reactants together in the right orientation, or briefly donate or accept charges. The reaction then runs thousands or millions of times faster.

An enzyme does not change how much energy the reaction releases or absorbs, and it comes out unchanged, ready to work again. It also does not make an endergonic reaction happen by itself. For that, cells couple it to an exergonic one, usually the hydrolysis of ATP.

Enzymes are sensitive to their surroundings. Each works best at a particular temperature and pH, and extreme conditions denature it. Cells also regulate enzymes with inhibitors and with molecules that bind allosteric sites. In feedback inhibition, a pathway's final product shuts down an early step, so the cell does not overproduce it.

q.q: Why doesn't sugar in a bowl spontaneously burn?
o: Activation energy is too high to overcome at room temperature

q.q: What does an enzyme NOT change?
o: The overall energy released by the reaction
